extracted.intended_audience: citizens and policymakers evaluating the U.S. Constitution's design for executive powers
extracted.subtask_description: Normative criteria and arguments for how executive powers (veto, command, pardons, treaties, appointments) should be allocated and constrained in a republican constitution. Focused on balancing decisiveness, responsibility, and checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualified negative (veto) instead of absolute negative
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of an absolute negative, give the Executive the qualified negative already described: return a bill for reconsideration, subject to being finally rejected only in the event of more than one third of each house concurring in the sufficiency of his objections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A qualified negative is more readily exercised than an absolute veto because it appears less harsh and is less apt to irritate; it encourages use (thus functioning as a practical check) and combines the executive's objections with the influence of a considerable proportion of the legislature. It reduces the chance that improper views will govern, compared to relying on a bare majority of the legislature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Veto mechanism should encourage reconsideration and coalition
rubrics_metrics.description: A man who might be afraid to defeat a law by his single veto might not scruple to return it for reconsideration; he would be encouraged by the reflection that if his opposition should prevail, it would embark in it a very respectable proportion of the legislative body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the veto to produce a deliberative effect: return-for-reconsideration mechanisms can harness legislative influence to support the executive's objections and restrain hasty or unjust majorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep judges distinct from executive functions
rubrics_metrics.description: The judges, who are to be the interpreters of the law, might receive an improper bias from having given a previous opinion in their revisionary capacities; by being often associated with the Executive, they might be induced to embark too far in the political views of that magistrate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid institutional arrangements that put judges in roles where they advise or share executive power; judicial independence is essential to prevent corruption or influence and to ensure impartial exposition of laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralize military command in a single executive (commander-in-chief)
rubrics_metrics.description: The President is to be 'commander-in-chief of the army and navy of the United States, and of the militia... when called into the actual service of the United States.' The direction of war most peculiarly demands those qualities which distinguish the exercise of power by a single hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: War requires unity of direction, secrecy, decision, and rapidity; these qualities argue for concentrating military authority in a single responsible executive rather than a council or legislature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pardoning power vested in the President, broadly unfettered (except impeachment)
rubrics_metrics.description: He is authorized to grant 'reprieves and pardons for offenses against the United States, except in cases of impeachment.' Humanity and good policy dictate that the benign prerogative of pardoning should be as little as possible fettered or embarrassed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single responsible person is better situated to weigh compassionate and discretionary considerations, and to act quickly in crises; undue legislative constraints would hamper timely mercy and restoration of public tranquillity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider legislative concurrence only as exception for treason
rubrics_metrics.description: The expediency of vesting the power of pardoning in the President has been contested only in relation to the crime of treason; it has been urged that this ought to depend on the assent of one or both branches of the legislature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While treason raises special concerns (because it is levelled at the being of society and may be connected with sedition), requiring legislative concurrence has pros and cons: it might prevent executive connivance but could impede timely clemency in insurrections and be subject to partisan bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pardons crucial in insurrection/rebellion because of timing
rubrics_metrics.description: In seasons of insurrection or rebellion, there are often critical moments when a well-timed offer of pardon to the insurgents or rebels may restore the tranquillity of the commonwealth; the dilatory process of convening the legislature would frequently be the occasion of letting slip the golden opportunity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grant the executive discretionary pardon power to act swiftly in emergencies where delay (even for days or hours) could make reconciliation or suppression impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treaty-making should be shared: President with Senate advice and consent (two-thirds present)
rubrics_metrics.description: The President is to have power, 'by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, to make treaties, provided two thirds of the senators present concur.' The joint possession of the power by President and Senate affords greater security than separate possession by either.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treaties are sui generis (neither strictly legislative nor executive); they demand executive qualities (negotiation, secrecy, dispatch) plus legislative participation because treaties have the force of law—so require a mixed agency to combine competency and democratic security.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude the House of Representatives from treaty formation
rubrics_metrics.description: The fluctuating and multitudinous composition of the House forbids us to expect in it those qualities which are essential: accurate and comprehensive knowledge of foreign politics; a steady and systematic adherence to the same views; decision, secrecy, and despatch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not involve large, frequently changing assemblies in treaty-making, as their size and character make them ill-suited to the secrecy, steadiness, and expedition required for foreign negotiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require two-thirds of members present (not two-thirds of whole) to avoid paralysis
rubrics_metrics.description: All provisions which require more than the majority have a tendency to embarrass operations; requiring two thirds of the whole number would in many cases from non-attendance amount to a necessity of unanimity. Requiring a proportion of attending members promotes punctuality and avoids practical paralysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set supermajority thresholds relative to those present to balance the need for a strong consensus with the need to keep government functional and avoid de facto unanimity caused by absences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nomination by President plus Senate advice and consent for appointments
rubrics_metrics.description: The President is 'to nominate, and, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, to appoint' principal officers; nomination exercises the President's judgment and, with Senate concurrence, secures both responsibility and a check against favoritism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mode combines the benefits of a single discerning nominator (responsibility, unity of judgment) with an independent body that restrains favoritism, promotes stability, and prevents purely partisan or personal appointments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nomination (vs sole appointment) preserves responsibility while avoiding abuses
rubrics_metrics.description: In the act of nomination, his judgment alone would be exercised; ... there can be no difference between nominating and appointing. The same motives which would influence a proper discharge of his duty in one case, would exist in the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vest nomination power in the executive to concentrate accountability; require confirmation so that rejection would reflect Senate scrutiny rather than opaque collusion, while preserving the executive's incentive to careful selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate concurrence as a check to prevent favoritism and promote administrative stability
rubrics_metrics.description: The necessity of their concurrence would have a powerful, though, in general, a silent operation. It would be an excellent check upon a spirit of favoritism in the President, and would tend greatly to prevent the appointment of unfit characters from State prejudice, family connection, or personal attachment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use confirmation as a preventive institutional guard: the possibility of rejection disciplines presidential nominations and links officer tenure to an independent body's approbation, discouraging wholesale patronage changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to fill vacancies during Senate recess (temporary commissions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The President shall have power to fill up all vacancies which may happen during the recess of the Senate, by granting commissions which shall expire at the end of their next session.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow temporary unilateral executive appointments to ensure continuity of government when the confirming body is not in session, while limiting their duration to preserve the confirmation check.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparent appointment procedures produce public responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: When appointments must be submitted to the judgment of an entire branch of the legislature, the circumstances attending an appointment naturally become matters of notoriety; the blame of a bad nomination would fall upon the President singly and absolutely; the censure of rejecting a good one would lie at the door of the Senate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design appointment mechanisms so that the public can identify actors and assign responsibility; opaque small councils (e.g., private councils making appointments) inhibit accountability and invite cabal and intrigue.
